full_text:
Stanford University is facing backlash after its Residential & Dining Enterprises used a photograph of students that had been edited by artificial intelligence—including entirely changing one Hispanic, male student into a Black woman—in its advertising.

The photo first came to light in a report by The Stanford Review, the university’s right-leaning student newspaper. The original image shows a female student on the left and two male students to her left, with all three smiling at the camera and posing with their food outside Star Ginger, a food stall in one of Stanford’s dining halls; the AI-edited image removed the rightmost male student and generated a Black woman in his place.

According to the Review and other news sources, the student who was edited out is Billy Ramirez, a junior studying human biology, according to his LinkedIn profile. Ramirez told the Review he was shocked when his friends sent him the edited image. The original photo was taken in 2024.

“At first, I found it hilarious that they had used AI to completely change our appearances, including my race and gender. But after looking at the comparison, I was also upset because I don’t agree with Stanford making those choices about how we were represented,” he said. “Seeing my identity changed and being left out of the picture made me feel, in a way, silenced and erased from a representation that was supposed to include me.”

In an emailed statement, Stanford spokesperson Charlene Gage wrote that the incident violates Stanford’s AI policies and that the banners containing the altered image have been taken down.

“Stanford’s AI policy is clear: The use of AI in producing or altering images of Stanford people, events, research, facilities, or achievements is strictly prohibited. Both the alteration and lack of disclosure in this case violate that policy. We are working to provide additional training for all staff and ensure proper review of all materials,” Gage wrote.

The AI also made other changes, like slightly altering the other two students’ faces, making the words “Stanford University” clearer on the female student’s sweatshirt and removing a pair of headphones hanging around the center male student’s neck. The AI-generated Black woman appears to be wearing a Stanford sweatshirt, whereas Ramirez was wearing a Gap sweatshirt.

title: The Future of the American University, According to Cornell Faculty
summary:
The Future of the American University, According to Cornell Faculty Katherine Knott Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM A Cornell committee made nearly 70 recommendations that it says will reorient the university to its core purpose. Byline(s) Katherine Knott The Future of the American University, According to Cornell Faculty
Katherine Knott Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM

A Cornell committee made nearly 70 recommendations that it says will reorient the university to its core purpose.

Byline(s)
Katherine Knott
full_text:
As higher education contends with seismic upheaval, the university cannot remain “exactly as it is today,” faculty at Cornell University said in a new report that outlines how the Ivy League institution can weather the current storms and “prepare for those that we cannot yet predict.”

The report resembles attempts from faculty at Vanderbilt and Yale Universities to diagnose what ails higher education and to chart a course forward. Unlike the Yale and Vanderbilt reports, the Cornell faculty largely contained their discussion to their own university, though they noted that they hope the commitments and recommendations inspire other institutions.

Cornell Provost Kavita Bala convened an interdisciplinary committee of faculty last fall to explore how the university should change over the next 50 years and specifically adapt to three disruptions: rapid technological change, fissures in the relationship between universities and the federal government, and the erosion of public trust in higher education. The results of that 18-person committee’s work were released Tuesday in a 238-page report and a condensed 17-page vision statement.

“The committee’s central premise is that the wave of disruption challenging higher education today is not a passing threat driven by transient forces,” the panel wrote in the vision statement. “Tensions between universities and the federal government are symptoms of larger, longer-term systemic issues that have arisen over decades. The future of the American university lies in leadership that recommits to a clear purpose, which the committee defines as promoting a human-centered, integrated learning ecosystem to cultivate sound judgment.”

Urgency was a key theme throughout both documents, as the committee noted that the work ahead won’t be easy but is necessary.

“Today’s pressures are too intense and the opportunities too promising to prioritize nostalgia over envisioning the future,” the committee wrote.

The committee made nearly 70 recommendations about how to reorient the university to that core purpose. They range from the broad—promoting whole-person education—to the specific, such as establishing a task force to develop a new tuition model, reconsidering the dissertation in doctoral programs and exploring a subscription model for lifelong learning.

The committee also recommended that Cornell create the Future of the American University Forum to build on the report’s recommendations, and further the discussion about where Cornell and higher education go from here.

“The questions raised by this committee cannot be resolved by a single report,” the wrote. “They require an institutional home that can sustain discussion, turn inquiry into action, and then transform the results of actions back into inquiry.”

Throughout the report, the committee stressed the need to connect the work of Cornell, a land-grant institution, with the public and focus on community engagement.

“At Cornell, public engagement and impact are woven into our DNA,” the committee wrote. “In challenging times such as these, it could be tempting to lean away from this commitment. It is exactly the opposite that Cornell must do, not only to regain public trust, but also to fulfill our purpose of putting knowledge to work in communities.”

Bala endorsed the report in a Tuesday statement and said the university will work on a strategic plan to translate the recommendations into action. She intends to share more concrete steps in the coming weeks.

“Throughout the committee’s work, one fundamental question rose to the top: ‘Is a university education still worth it?’ The committee’s answer is a resounding yes—if we clarify and renew the university’s purpose,” she said.

title: Colleges Adopted ‘Systemic Suppression’ of Protesters, New Investigation Shows
summary:
Colleges Adopted ‘Systemic Suppression’ of Protesters, New Investigation Shows jessica.blake@… Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM Drawing on records, media reports and surveys, the ACLU and Amnesty International USA break down how colleges have “disproportionately” violated the rights of pro-Palestinian students. Byline(s) Jessica Blake Colleges Adopted ‘Systemic Suppression’ of Protesters, New Investigation Shows
jessica.blake@… Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM

Drawing on records, media reports and surveys, the ACLU and Amnesty International USA break down how colleges have “disproportionately” violated the rights of pro-Palestinian students.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
Government officials and university administrators took “heavy-handed” and “excessive” actions in response to campus protests after Oct. 7, 2023, actions that “disproportionately targeted” pro-Palestinian students and faculty members, creating a chilling effect that will stifle political expression for years to come, a new report says.

Produced by the American Civil Liberties Union and Amnesty International USA, the 287-page report documents what it calls the “systemic suppression” of anti-genocide speech at colleges and universities across the country. The “McCarthyite censorship” against individuals who exercised their right to free speech and criticized the Israeli government for the nation’s protracted war in Gaza continues to this day, the authors argue.

“Universities’ responses to campus-related Palestine advocacy and pro-Palestinian demonstrations have been more punitive in comparison with their historical responses to other comparable demonstrations over decades,” the report says. As a result, “These universities directly or indirectly have made it easier for the Trump administration to crack down on student activism, causing long-term damage to higher education.”

Based on a two-year investigation, the report covers events, policies and practices that have unfolded since the terror attacks of Oct. 7 at 80 public and private colleges and universities across 28 states and Washington, D.C. It draws on college records, statements from government agencies and officials, court records, case law, media reports, and survey responses from students who participated in protests at 41 colleges. (Ninety-six individuals completed the survey.)

To illustrate their arguments, the ACLU and Amnesty International zoomed in on six institutions: Columbia University; City College of New York; Tulane University; the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Michigan; and the University of Texas at Austin. They also include in-depth case studies of a handful of international student protesters the Trump administration targeted with arrest, detention and/or deportation, including former Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil and Tufts University Ph.D. student Rümeysa Öztürk.

Collectively, the findings show that “hundreds, if not thousands, of students at universities nationwide have faced campus disciplinary proceedings,” sometimes as severe as suspensions or expulsions—though it’s impossible to know the exact count, as many colleges have kept their disciplinary processes under wraps, the report notes. The targeting of pro-Palestinian students and faculty has led to “a steep decline in protests and a less visible protest movement on campuses across the country,” it concludes.

The report echoes the findings of a previous Inside Higher Ed analysis, which shows similar trends of stifled free speech, particularly in support of left-wing causes.

“These punishments can impose severe and lifelong consequences and profoundly disrupt students’ lives and academic careers,” the report authors write. “Instead of targeting students and faculty who are expressing their right to protest and association, higher education institutions have a responsibility to protect these rights. The First Amendment compels public universities and colleges to respect free speech rights and some have failed these obligations.”

The report states that more than 1,360 pro-Palestinian student demonstrations took place in the United States between Oct. 7, 2023, and May 3, 2024—97 percent of which remained peaceful. It details how many prompted forceful responses from campus police or local law enforcement summoned by university administrators, citing reporting showing that protesters were detained at more than 70 institutions; police arrested more than 3,200 people on campuses.

The punishment didn’t end there. Since the period covered in the report, colleges have continued to censor expression that criticizes Israel and to enforce campus codes of conduct against pro-Palestinian student activists. The nonprofit group Palestine Legal reported that in 2025, it received 663 requests for legal assistance in cases in which university administrations were investigating or had imposed sanctions for campus-related Palestine advocacy—up from 580 in 2024. In many cases, the report says, university enforcement of campus policy was “selective” and “far beyond what universities have historically imposed for similar acts of civil disobedience.”

The authors argue that much of the disciplinary action came as a result of pressure from the government and donors. They also criticize universities for adopting the “overly broad” definition of antisemitism outlined by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, which includes “denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination” and “drawing comparisons of contemporary Israeli policy to that of the Nazis.” The report contends that such speech is protected by the First Amendment.

“Speech that is critical of Israel cannot, alone, constitute harassment,” the report says. “Campus policies incorporating the IHRA definition of antisemitism misconstrue antidiscrimination law to censor and stifle campus speech.” And while universities have often cited complying with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act—which bans discrimination based on race, color or national origin in federally funded programs—as a reason for dismantling pro-Palestinian protests, the reports’ authors say the IHRA definition goes “far beyond” what Title VI requires.

Between the spring and fall terms of 2024, the total number of protest actions dropped by more than 64 percent, the report notes, and protests have continued to decline since. Yet support for the people of Gaza has actually grown: According to a March 2025 Gallup poll, sympathy for Palestinians had reached a record high, while U.S. support for Israel had reached its lowest level in at least 25 years.

Among other recommendations, the report calls on university leaders to apply campus conduct codes and protest policies “fairly and neutrally to all students” and to “resist” pressures applied by the federal government.

That means upholding free speech protections for all students and scholars, regardless of nationality, ethnicity or race; ensuring that students have ample channels for expression on campus and that law enforcement is used only as a measure of last resort; and refraining from adopting policies that rely on overly broad and vague definitions.

“We urge universities and college administrators to resist the temptation to silence students or faculty members because powerful voices deem their views offensive. Instead, we urge them to defend the university’s core mission of encouraging debate, fostering free-flowing inquiry, and preparing the future leaders of our pluralistic society to tolerate even profound differences of opinion,” the report says.

title: ED Redirects $235M in MSI Funds to HBCUs, Tribal Colleges
summary:
ED Redirects $235M in MSI Funds to HBCUs, Tribal Colleges Ryan Quinn Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM Byline(s) Ryan Quinn ED Redirects $235M in MSI Funds to HBCUs, Tribal Colleges
Ryan Quinn Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Ryan Quinn
full_text:
The Education Department announced Tuesday that it is sending more than $174 million to historically Black colleges and universities and $61 million to tribal colleges. It says the “one-time” investments come from programs that generally funded Hispanic-serving and other minority-serving institutions—the same way it provided a similar boost to HBCUs and tribal colleges last year.

Last September, ED abruptly canceled grants for most minority-serving institutions, saying those programs were unconstitutionally discriminatory because they require colleges to enroll a certain percentage of students from a particular racial or ethnic background to qualify. ED then redirected $495 million to HBCUs and tribal colleges. In December, the Justice Department backed up ED’s legal interpretation.

On Tuesday, ED told Inside Higher Ed that it has urged Congress to fix the constitutional issues, and for now it has worked with the White House Office of Management and Budget to identify legal options for the funds. Congress blocked the department from defunding the MSI programs entirely, but it allowed the agency to move the money into the Strengthening Institutions Program.

This year, the money for HBCUs is from a grant program for Hispanic-serving institutions aimed at boosting the number of Hispanic and low-income students in the STEM fields and developing model transfer and articulation agreements between two- and four-year institutions in such fields, the Education Department said. Tribal colleges are getting about $14.4 million from the STEM program.

The other $47.2 million for tribal colleges is from a different batch of programs aimed at strengthening Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian–serving institutions; Asian American– and Native American Pacific Islander–serving institutions; and Native American–serving nontribal institutions.

Education Secretary Linda McMahon said Tuesday in a news release that “for nearly 200 years, HBCUs have been engines of opportunity in communities, advancing critical innovations and uplifting local industries across the nation. This new investment will help ensure these vital institutions have the resources they need to continue delivering world-class education and to prepare students for success in a rapidly evolving economy.”

Moriah O’Brien, vice president of congressional and federal relations at the American Indian Higher Education Consortium, said, “We don’t advocate to take money away from anyone else,” but repeatedly expressed gratitude for the added funds for tribal colleges. She said they “can be a catalyst for incredible things.”

Tribal colleges and universities are underfunded, lack large donor networks and often don’t have on-campus housing, she said, and many students take classes in repurposed portable buildings.

“This represents so much promise and possibility, and giving the TCUs the opportunity to build on the one-time increase they had last year means a tremendous amount,” O’Brien said.

The Thurgood Marshall College Fund, which represents public HBCUs, welcomed the extra funding with “sincere gratitude” in a news release.

“Today’s announcement builds upon that track record of support for our historically Black Colleges and universities that President Trump has demonstrated since the start of his first term in 2017,” said TMCF President and CEO Harry L. Williams. “This result would not have been possible without a commitment from HBCU advocates to work in a bipartisan manner to communicate the value of our institutions to all elected and appointed leaders. We applaud the Trump administration for doubling down on their investments into HBCUs as we build the workforce and develop the leaders that will solidify our nation’s global competitiveness for decades to come.”

title: Conn. State System Scandal Drives Demands for Reform
summary:
Conn. State System Scandal Drives Demands for Reform Josh Moody Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM A report found Connecticut State Colleges and Universities mishandled misconduct allegations against a former chancellor. Now state lawmakers are threatening action. Byline(s) Josh Moody Conn. State System Scandal Drives Demands for Reform
Josh Moody Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM

A report found Connecticut State Colleges and Universities mishandled misconduct allegations against a former chancellor. Now state lawmakers are threatening action.

Byline(s)
Josh Moody
full_text:
When Connecticut State Colleges and Universities Interim Chancellor John Maduko resigned in April after 10 months on the job, officials noted he stepped down amid an investigation into a policy violation. Now an independent report has revealed that the system failed to adequately respond to multiple allegations of sexually inappropriate conduct by Maduko toward women working in the system.

The report also found that the board ignored basic vetting practices in elevating Maduko, who had previously served a roughly three-year stint as president of Connecticut State Community College.

Maduko is the second chancellor to leave in less than a year. His predecessor, Terrence Cheng, exited the role in June 2025 after the Board of Regents refused to renew his contract following a report that he spent lavishly on meals, alcohol and chauffeured rides to his home in New York.

Even as critics pounce on the report showing that the system mishandled the allegations against Maduko, another leadership controversy is brewing at a member institution: Employees have accused Central Connecticut State University President Zulma Toro of bullying and intimidation. The system opened an investigation into Toro last month.

As that investigation continues, state lawmakers and employees are raising alarm over the failure of the board to police misconduct at the top levels. And as their demands for reform grow, system officials have promised changes to current oversight practices.

Missed Warnings

The first complaints about Maduko date to fall 2022, months after he became president of the community college, when an administrator reported concerns about his treatment of women and rumors of inappropriate incidents. Additional complaints followed in 2024 and 2025, including allegations that he sent sexualized messages to women working in the system. Some employees told investigators they were reluctant to report his conduct due to concerns about retaliation.

(Contacted via LinkedIn, Maduko did not respond to a request for comment.)

Independent investigators found that regents and administrators within the system failed to uphold policies on handling sexual misconduct reports, noting that their response lacked “timeliness, safeguards, supportive measures, and appropriate communications, among other failings.” The report, released last week by the firm Grand River Solutions, also found that employees who experienced sexual harassment lacked trust in the reporting process, “in part due to concerns about how confidential information had been handled and potentially shared in the past.”

Investigators also concluded that the board did not adequately vet Maduko for the job.

Regents “did not perform a background check, review performance or personnel records, or obtain recommendations because Maduko was an internal candidate for an interim position and thus had already gone through a background check when first hired,” the investigation found.

Board leaders stepped down shortly after Maduko. Then-Board Chair Marty Guay resigned in May, days after complaints against Maduko became public. Guay said in his resignation announcement that he had already planned to leave but “now is the right time to step aside.”

System spokesperson Sam Norton said that CSCU accepted the findings of the Grand River Solutions report, which identified “serious issues involving accountability, reporting responsibilities, leadership decision-making, and institutional response,” and has begun working toward reforms.

“These actions will include strengthening employee reporting and escalation requirements, improving leadership screening and vetting, reinforcing compliance and training, reviewing governance and oversight practices, and taking appropriate personnel action,” Norton wrote in an emailed statement to Inside Higher Ed. “The report provides a clear roadmap for change. Our responsibility now is to implement those changes, hold ourselves accountable, and restore confidence in the systems that are intended to protect our students and employees.”

A Trail of Complaints

Complaints elsewhere in the system are fueling broader leadership concerns.

Last month, Lisa Bigelow, director of institutional advancement at Central Connecticut State University and president of the union that represents administrative employees in the state system, filed a complaint with the system’s Office of Compliance alleging that Toro routinely yelled at, intimidated and retaliated against her subordinates.

Bigelow accused Toro of verbally berating employees, including her, and asking staff members to perform personal errands, such as scheduling her medical appointments and watching her dog, according to a copy of the complaint that Bigelow shared with local media.

Current and former employees have also lodged several complaints against Toro since 2019.

Bigelow previously filed a complaint against the CCSU president with state auditors, also in 2019, alleging a “pattern of increasingly abusive and bullying behavior being exhibited by Dr. Toro.”

CCSU communications professor Serafin Mendez-Mendez also raised concerns about Toro’s behavior in his own complaint in 2019, according to local TV station WFSB. The news outlet reported that a former employee also emailed Cheng in 2021 to complain that Toro shamed, bullied and intimidated people she didn’t like but did not receive a response from the chancellor.

Central Connecticut State University referred a request for comment to the system.

Norton, the system spokesperson, told Inside Higher Ed by email that “CSCU takes all complaints seriously” and “acted immediately to initiate a formal process” after officials received the allegations.

“The investigation, opened August 20, 2026, is now underway and no findings have been made,” Norton wrote. “It is important that we allow the established process to work and that we not prejudge either the facts or the appropriate employment action before those facts have been fully assessed. As this is an ongoing personnel matter, we cannot comment further at this time.”

Calls for Reform

Though CSCU has pledged to make changes on its own, that may not be enough for lawmakers.

State Senator Gary Winfield, a Democrat and chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, was one of multiple lawmakers who castigated the system for what he called a betrayal of public trust.

“What’s before us in this report is not a simple policy-related failure; we’re dealing with a failure of basic human decency and leadership,” he said in a statement last week that followed the release of the report. “The report gives the appearance of cover-ups and people who are more worried about themselves than the people they’re supposed to serve. Connecticut residents don’t fund state institutions of higher education to serve as a shield or cover for abuse.”

While Winfield noted that the board chair resigned in the wake of the Maduko scandal, he suggested the Legislature “should weigh the possibility of changes to the state Board of Regents” next year.

State Senator Derek Slap and State Representative Gregg Haddad, co-chairs of the Higher Education and Employment Advancement Committee, also released a statement signed by 10 other Democratic lawmakers calling for “a significant change in workplace culture, better safeguards and training and an end to the abuse of power, resources and taxpayer dollars.”

When the Legislature reconvenes, so will the work to hold the system accountable, they said.

“The Higher Education Committee passed legislation increasing accountability and transparency for the entire system and we stand ready to continue that work in January,” the group of lawmakers wrote in a statement last week. “This is another data point that indicates the system has not been working as intended and we are prepared to consider all options moving forward.”

title: Out Now: 2026 Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers
summary:
Out Now: 2026 Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers colleen.flaherty Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM Byline(s) IHE Staff Out Now: 2026 Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers
colleen.flaherty Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
IHE Staff
full_text:
Provosts are confident in their role and their relationship with their president, according to the 2026 Inside Higher Ed/Hanover Research Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers, out today (N=376). But, like last year, resources are a sticking point. In 2026, not quite half of provosts (47 percent) say they have what they need to actually implement initiatives. Provosts nevertheless trend optimistic about their institutions’ futures, though 13 percent signal near-term threats to their colleges’ ability to carry out their academic missions and 18 percent signal active financial distress.

Regarding the future of higher education broadly, just a quarter of provosts (25 percent) are at least somewhat confident that the U.S. university research enterprise will remain strong over the next decade. This increases to 43 percent among public doctoral university provosts, despite their disproportionate experience with recent federal funding cuts, which is also reflected in the survey.

In write-in comments about underappreciated challenges, provosts flag topics from doing more with less to student readiness levels. Wrote one provost: “How to be adaptable and responsive to a changing society with increasingly constrained resources.” Some also describe the slate of recent policy changes as unfunded mandates that are increasing compliance costs without increasing quality.

“Federal and state regulations meant to curb bad actors are extra burdensome to smaller colleges where everyone in administration already wears multiple hats,” wrote another provost. “The extra steps toward compliance decrease efficiency and increase cost—with no real added benefit to our students, who were already well served and very satisfied.” Just 17 percent of provosts predict that the planned federal accreditation overhaul will have any kind of positive effect on higher ed.

Most provosts (82 percent) rate their institution’s academic health as good or excellent, and most also affirm the value of general education and the liberal arts. Looking deeper, however, just 49 percent are confident that quality is consistent across their institution’s degree programs. As for work-integrated learning, limited staff capacity to manage these opportunities—not employer partner interest or faculty buy-in—is the top reported barrier to expansion, for 69 percent of provosts. While a majority of all provosts are reasonably confident in digital learning—63 percent believe in the quality of their institution’s online and hybrid course offerings, for instance—fewer (35 percent) describe the technology infrastructure around nondegree credentials as robust.

AI’s return on investment so far is more about efficiency than deep change, with more provosts pointing to clear institutional gains in individual employee productivity (39 percent) over those in areas such as teaching and learning (29 percent) or research (7 percent). Only 8 percent describe operational transformation. Provosts themselves report significant AI uptake—seven in 10 (71 percent) say they use it for summarizing documents or reports, for example—but staff capacity and skills (51 percent) and outright faculty or staff resistance (50 percent) are the biggest reported limitations on AI’s impact institutionwide.

Governance approaches are scattered, and just one in five provosts agrees (17 percent) or strongly agrees (3 percent) that their institution has a coherent vision for how AI will change what it teaches and how to teach it. Still, few provosts (8 percent) indicate that their institution is taking a primarily defensive approach to AI and assessment at this point.

title: From AI Use to Funding Cuts: How Provosts Are Navigating 2026
summary:
From AI Use to Funding Cuts: How Provosts Are Navigating 2026 Emma Whitford Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM Inside Higher Ed’s annual CAO survey reveals a fractured landscape, where academic leaders rely on personal AI tools amid broader technological and political disruption. Byline(s) Emma Whitford From AI Use to Funding Cuts: How Provosts Are Navigating 2026
Emma Whitford Wed, 09/23/2026 - 03:00 AM

Inside Higher Ed’s annual CAO survey reveals a fractured landscape, where academic leaders rely on personal AI tools amid broader technological and political disruption.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
As artificial intelligence continues to disrupt college campuses, chief academic officers are embracing AI tools. Roughly seven in 10 provosts use AI in their own day-to-day work at least once per week, according to Inside Higher Ed’s latest survey of CAOs—but only one in 10 reported their institution has a centralized AI strategy.

Provosts report that AI has most delivered value to their institution in the form of individual productivity gains (39 percent said this) and administrative efficiency (36 percent), which is reflected in how they most often use the technology. Seventy-one percent of provosts use AI to summarize documents and reports, 66 percent for presentations and meetings, and 65 percent to draft communications to faculty, staff or students. One survey respondent noted they receive more than 100 emails per day and use AI to “identify high-priority action items” in their inbox. Others said they use AI to help source data from other institutions, for calendar analysis, grant development and organizing higher ed news.

Inside Higher Ed’s 2026 Survey of College and University Chief Academic Officers, released today, includes responses from 376 CAOs at mostly public and private nonprofit, two- and four-year institutions who were polled in July and August. In addition to taking their pulse on AI, Inside Higher Ed and Hanover Research asked provosts about the rapidly changing federal and state policy landscape; tenure, shared governance and academic freedom; faculty and staff retention; and academic program health and institutional effectiveness, among other topics.

Most of the presidents I know would either publicly agree or confidentially agree, the provost has the hardest job in higher ed.”

—Paul LeBlanc, former university president and author of Reclaiming Purpose: The University in an AI World

Paul LeBlanc, former president of Southern New Hampshire University and author of the new book Reclaiming Purpose: The University in an AI World, said he was not surprised to see that so many provosts now utilize AI tools in their own work.

“Most of the presidents I know would either publicly agree or confidentially agree, the provost has the hardest job in higher ed,” he said. Indeed, fewer than half of CAOs—47 percent—said they have adequate resources to implement initiatives in their role.

“If you think of the sheer volume of information the provost typically has to process in a given week, it’s enormous,” LeBlanc said. “So, from an information-management perspective, you can see why [AI] would be very appealing.”

For most provosts, AI’s clearest returns end with their own personal use; only 12 percent of respondents said that institutional AI investment has resulted in department workflow optimization, and only 8 percent reported “institutionwide operational transformation.” Fifteen percent of all provosts—and 28 percent of provosts at private nonprofit baccalaureate institutions—said their institution hasn’t invested in AI at all.

This discrepancy is in part due to the way people most often use AI, LeBlanc said.

“When you bolt AI onto existing workflows, there is limited impact,” he said. “When you use AI to rethink how the work happens, then you get more profound impacts … I don’t think there are a lot of universities that are deploying AI in that way, where they’re rethinking the whole system.”

One in five provosts agreed or strongly agreed that their institution has a coherent vision for how AI will change what it teaches and how to teach that. Thirty-one percent of public doctoral provosts agreed with this, while only 11 percent of private nonprofit baccalaureate provosts and 12 percent of community college provosts did.

Asked about current AI uses, 54 percent of CAOs said their institution uses virtual AI assistants and chatbots. Up from 50 percent last year, this remains the top institutional use. About four in 10 provosts said their institution uses AI for research and data analysis, up from 31 percent last year, while 39 percent use AI for administrative processes such as scheduling—up from 24 percent. Among the least frequent uses are fundraising (11 percent), personalized learning (8 percent) and facilities management (4 percent).

Institutionwide AI impact is limited by skills and staff capacity, 51 percent of CAOs reported (as did 55 percent of chief technology officers in Inside Higher Ed’s May CTO survey). Exactly half of provosts named faculty and staff resistance as a limiting factor, and 39 percent cited concerns about how AI affects students. Nearly three in 10 provosts pointed to cost as an issue.

Students’ use of AI—for better and for worse—has dominated higher ed headlines over the past year, as institutions rethink how to assess students’ comprehension and mastery when AI agents can complete many traditional college assignments and AI-assisted cheating incidents abound. Only 8 percent of CAOs reported that their institution’s approach to AI at this point is “primarily defensive,” defined as focused on preventing and detecting cheating. About 13 percent said their institution is primarily focused on adapting current assignments and tests in response to AI, and 20 percent described their institution’s approach as “primarily generative,” meaning that it is actively rethinking what it assesses and how.

Over all, provosts’ attitudes toward the technology remain mixed. Nearly half of provosts—48 percent—rate AI’s impact on higher ed as neither positive nor negative. About 28 percent say its impact has been positive, and 17 percent say it’s been negative.

More Federal Influence, Less Funding

Like last year, Inside Higher Ed asked provosts about how the changing federal policy landscape under the second Trump administration has impacted their institution and their work. Funding remains a major concern: Half of all provosts reported that federal funding to their college or university has declined under Trump 2.0. Three in five CAOs at public institutions and four in five CAOs at public doctoral universities, in particular, said this. Just 3 percent of all provosts reported any kind of funding increase.

Some 42 percent of provosts reporting cuts (n=183) said federal funding has declined between 5 and 10 percent under Trump 2.0. Almost a quarter of impacted provosts reported funding declines over 10 percent—up from 12 percent the year prior.

In response to such changes, nearly half of all CAOs said their institution has pursued alternative funding sources. Another 29 percent said it has restructured or scaled back programs that relied on specific grants, and a quarter reduced staff positions. About one in 10 provosts reported postponed facilities projects and 7 percent said their institution partnered with others to share resources. Earlier this spring, reports of canceled or delayed graduate admissions at some colleges and universities prompted concerns of a draining Ph.D. pool, but in this most recent survey, only 4 percent of CAOs said their institution had paused or reduced graduate student admissions in response to federal funding changes.

To make up for declining research funding, specifically, some provosts said their institution is diversifying funding sources (31 percent), developing more industry partnerships (24 percent) and expanding grant-writing support (17 percent). Only 4 percent reported that their institution is reducing research expectations.

Amid all of the funding uncertainty, a quarter of all provosts said they are “somewhat” or “very confident” that the U.S. research enterprise will remain strong over the next decade. Though provosts at public doctoral institutions more frequently reported funding declines of more than 10 percent, they were more optimistic—43 percent said the research enterprise would likely remain strong.

Terry Brown, vice president of academic innovation and transformation at the American Association of State Colleges and Universities, and a former university provost, attributed this confidence to a higher starting point. “Doctoral institutions have a stronger base of research support to begin with, so they may be in a position to be more resilient,” she said.

About four in 10 provosts also said that federal policymakers have increased their influence on academic decision-making over the last two years. That figure rose to 46 percent among public university provosts, versus 35 percent of their private university peers.

“We are seeing an effort by the federal government to exert influence over academic decision-making, such as curriculum, research projects and faculty personnel decisions, through two major levers it holds: federal funding and accreditation,” Brown said. “Apart from the fact that most Americans do not want the federal government to control these areas of higher education, such intrusions can vary from one administration to the next, depending on who is in power.”

As the Trump administration overhauls accreditation nationwide, only 17 percent of provosts said the reforms would have a somewhat or strongly positive impact on higher ed. Provosts at community colleges and Southern institutions were more likely to say this, with 29 percent and 35 percent saying the reforms would be positive, respectively. Only 11 percent of provosts at private nonprofit baccalaureate institutions and 6 percent at Northeastern institutions said the same.

About a quarter of provosts reported their institution has modified language in course descriptions or program materials in response to recent federal policy changes or actions. Another quarter said it has reviewed and modified international student programming—up from the 16 percent who said so a year prior. About a fifth of provosts reported changing department names or descriptions, and 11 percent made revisions to curricular content in “politically sensitive areas.”

Brown said she’s seen AASCU member institutions taking all of these actions and more. “Our members have been grappling with understanding exactly what is required of them by law,” she said.

Lukewarm on Tenure

Nearly half of provosts—48 percent—said academic freedom at their institution is “strong and well protected, despite external pressure,” up from 36 percent last year. Another 44 percent reported that academic freedom is “generally maintained but with increasing challenges.” Only 5 percent said it’s “under significant strain from multiple directions.”

These numbers vary by region. Two-thirds of CAOs at Northeastern institutions said academic freedom is well protected, while one-third of CAOs at Southern institutions said the same. Meanwhile, 57 percent of Southern institution CAOs said academic freedom is generally maintained but with increasing challenges. Southern institutions include colleges and universities in Alabama, Florida and Texas, where public institutions have increasingly battled state interference in academic affairs.

Tim Cain, an academic freedom expert and professor of higher education at the University of Georgia, hesitated to put too much confidence in provosts’ assessments of academic freedom.

“I am not convinced that most provosts have a pulse on their faculty and understand how both the broader climate and specific actions are affecting and limiting the work of faculty,” Cain said. “Especially at larger institutions, but at most institutions, provosts are somewhat distant from the day-to-day work of faculty … There is also a larger tendency to deflect and believe that things are OK here but are a problem elsewhere.”

As tenure continues to receive increased scrutiny from politicians, administrators and the general public, fewer than half of provosts—45 percent—said tenure is “very” or “extremely important” to the health of their institution. Last year, 53 percent said this. Responses to this question vary widely by institution type in 2026: Provosts at public doctoral institutions largely agreed with tenure’s importance (72 percent), while provosts at associate and private nonprofit doctoral and master’s institutions did not (28 percent and 29 percent, respectively). In place of tenure, 53 percent of all provosts said they favor long-term faculty contracts.

“Tenure has been and remains the most robust protection for academic freedom, even if it does not protect everything that some faculty believe,” Cain said. He is skeptical about how well long-term faculty contracts would protect academic freedom: The strength of the contract would depend greatly on its terms and length, he said.

“Long-term contracts might just delay a dismissal,” he explained, “as they might not require an affirmative act of dismissal but allow a faculty member deemed problematic—including because a student, politician or donor complained about their research or teaching—to be administratively nonrenewed.”

Provosts are also paying attention to faculty attrition. Thirty percent of provosts in the South and 27 percent in the Midwest report higher-than-usual faculty turnover, compared with 17 percent in the Northeast and 19 percent in the West. Still, the overall share of provosts reporting increased faculty turnover has chilled since the Great Resignation.

This year, provosts cited competitive offers elsewhere (64 percent) and natural career progression (45 percent), followed by significant family or life events (34 percent), burnout (33 percent) and insufficient resources for the job (27 percent), as the most frequent causes of faculty turnover. Just 12 percent attributed turnover to the political climate in their state or region—though that figure increased to 18 percent of provosts in the Midwest and 15 percent of those in the South, versus 1 percent of provosts in the Northeast and 7 percent in the West.

title: Elections in Brazil: a subdued, digital campaign heightens uncertainty about the results
summary: A political scientist analyzes the uncertain outlook for this year’s elections and the risks their results pose to governability and democracy in Brazil.
full_text:
With less than two weeks to go before voters head to the polls on Oct. 4, 2026, Brazil is experiencing a presidential election campaign that is much less heated than many would expect given the high-level of polarization in the country.

The latest polling also suggest few shifts in the political landscape, dominated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his main right-wing challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of incarcerated former President Jair Bolsonaro.

But making predictions about Brazil’s presidential vote is a tricky business. In Brazil, voting is mandatory for literate citizens between 18 and 70 years of age, and if one presidential candidate doesn’t get to 50%+1 of the valid votes (not counting absentees and blank or invalid votes) in the first round, the field is narrowed to two candidates, who then face a run-off, scheduled for Oct. 25, 2026.

The run-off is a very likely scenario in the current situation. But as a political scientist who has studied Brazilian elections for decades, I don’t think it’s safe at the moment to base analyses on existing second-round simulations, since about 30% of voters are still undecided in the first round, if spontaneous polls are to be trusted. Spontaneous polls ask voters who they would vote for without presenting them a list of candidates, and they historically indicate a number of undecided voters closer to the actual figure.

The average of the last 18 polls conducted through Sept. 22 shows 39.4% support for incumbent President Lula and 33.6% for Flávio Bolsonaro. This is not much different from the latest Quaest poll, released on Sept. 21, which found 37% for Lula and 33% for Flávio Bolsonaro.

When examined from the perspective of an average percentage, the figures from these 18 polls indicate that 27% of voters are undecided, according to the spontaneous responses. The Quaest poll found a higher figure: 35% undecided. Let’s say, then, that undecided voters fall within the range of 30% to 35%. This is a high degree of indecision so close to the election.

Thus, I’m working on the assumption that this relative stability in the polls — fluctuating within the margin of error — and the high percentage of undecided voters point to a very lackluster campaign. And in fact, there isn’t much activity on the streets; I’m not seeing the number of flags or stickers I did in previous campaigns.

A lackluster online campaign

I have two additional hypotheses to explain this lack of enthusiasm. The first is that neither Lula nor Flávio Bolsonaro are inspiring Brazilians to get out and campaign on the streets. Even within each candidate’s own echo chamber, there appears to be many doubts over their ability to enthuse would-be supporters.

The second is that the 2026 election campaign is playing out mainly through digital platforms. And a campaign that’s mostly online reduces face-to-face interaction and dampens the energy of impromptu moments at rallies. Voters wonder whether what they see on social media is reality or merely what algorithms have filtered for them. Social media has this ability to form crystallized bubbles that stifle debate.

This is clearly evident in the polls when they break down voting intentions by political orientation. Among Lula supporters, 91% choose Lula. And among Bolsonaro supporters, 90% back Flávio Bolsonaro. On the non-Lula left, 78% say they will vote for Lula. On the non-Bolsonaro right, 67% support Flávio Bolsonaro. Those who identify as independent are split. This is what the figures from the Sept. 21 Quaest poll show.

In the same Quaest poll, when asked if their choice for the first round might change, 79% say their decisions are final, while 21% say they may still switch candidates. These 21% who may change their vote from what they are thinking at present suggests that volatility is likely to be high this year, and that many voters will wait until the last minute to decide. This is likely to maintain the atmosphere of uncertainty that has characterized the current presidential campaign right up to the last minute.

The ‘vote for the winner’ hypothesis

But there is an additional piece of data in the latest Quaest poll that could affect this uncertainty. When asked who is likely to win the election, 55% say Lula - far exceeding the percentage of respondents who say they will vote for him. Meanwhile, 30% believe Flávio Bolsonaro will win, roughly inline with current voting intentions.

This discrepancy between voting intention and who voters think will win could be crucial. Historically, there has been a group of voters who tend to favor the winning candidate in the second round. The indications are, at the moment, this may ultimately favor Lula. The serving president may also benefit from pragmatic choices: between the untested Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula, the incumbent who is already at the helm and holds few surprises in store.

Flávio Bolsonaro, however, can capitalize on his last name. Despite his legal problems since leaving office in 2023, Jair Bolsonaro remains popular among his right-wing base. In addition, there are some Brazilians who are turned off by the political longevity of Lula, who first became president in 2003.

One thing is certain: this will once again be a close election. And it will likely be decided by independent voters, who are currently still very divided between the two main candidates.

The election results will also be affected by voter alienation. The higher the abstention rate and the number of invalid votes, the greater the impact on the final result.

September or October shocks?

And what about the very likely runoff on Oct. 25? As a political scientist, I always treat second-rounds as a new election, with a short and intense campaign that tends to be more heated than the first round. But I make no predictions about it before knowing the result of the first round of voting.

The reality in Brazil is politics can be volatile. There is a great deal of compromising information at the heart of ongoing investigations, such as the Banco Master case, centering around a banking fraud that has drawn in a lot of high-profile poltiical figures. The outcome of the related crisis at the Federal Supreme Court – which has pitted a Jair Bolsonaro appointed Justice, André Mendonça, against the Lula-backed Alexandre de Moraes – may also influence voters’ choices. Or it may not.

Polling also doesn’t take into account how the events of Jan. 8, 2023, and the entire coup plot that preceded it, may influence voters when it comes down to making a final decision.

If these events – during which pro-Bolsonaro supporters stormed government buildings in the capital and attempted to oust the newly elected Lula – remain fresh in voters’ minds, or if they are brought up again during the campaign, they could also be a deciding factor. Especially since Flávio Bolsonaro is promising amnesty to those convicted, including his father.

The crisis of coalition presidential system

The current field of presidential candidates – 14 in total – also reveals various aspects of the crisis in Brazil’s coalition presidential system – something that began under the Bolsonaro administration. Parliamentary amendments to the federal budget totaling tens of billions of dollars gave members of the Brazilian parliament’s two houses – the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate – the autonomy to channel funds to their constituencies without needing authorization from the executive branch. The result was less incentive to support presidential candidates or join the governing coalition.

This crisis is directly linked to the vote — not just for president, but for the House and the Senate. A new rule governing amendments will depend on congressional approval. And only the popular vote can alter the balance of power that currently grants a legislative majority to a much-criticized group of parties called “centrão,” or “big center.”

The importance of the congressional election

If the vote for the House of Representatives and the Senate maintains the current status quo, it will make it very difficult for the winning presidential candidate to form an effective and responsible coalition between Congress and the federal government — one willing to change the current rules on amendments to help ensure the country’s governability.

Therefore, there is a great deal at stake as Brazilians prepare to vote — from reaffirming democracy to defending governability.

Lula has been accused by his critics of being a poor manager of the serving coalition. But his supporters present him as an experienced politician, and a skilled negotiator who understands the demands of the office of the chief executive, and grasps the political dynamics in Congress.

This is an election that could have a significant impact on the future of democracy and the well-being of Brazilian society. Yet these issues have failed to engage the electorate. And the lackluster campaign only heightens the sense of uncertainty leading into the election.

title: Advance HE publishes case studies celebrating innovation in small and specialist providers
summary: The post Advance HE publishes case studies celebrating innovation in small and specialist providers appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
16 projects tackling integrating AI, employability and inclusion feature in this year’s round of funding.

We are pleased to publish our latest collection of Innovative Practice Grants case studies, showcasing 16 projects from small, specialist, independent and college-based higher education (SSI/CBHE) providers across the UK. The work highlights practical, staff-led innovation from a wide range of institutions.

Our Innovative Practice Grants scheme invites SSI/CBHE member institutions to document initiatives that have had a demonstrable impact on staff or students. This year’s collection spans providers from Lakes College West Cumbria to ESCP Business School London and Ravensbourne University, London, covering themes from artificial intelligence in assessment to admissions reform, industry partnerships and inclusive teaching.

Authentic assessment in the AI-era

Several projects tackle the challenge of integrating AI without letting it do students’ thinking for them. At Lakes College West Cumbria, a redesigned assessment on a nuclear decommissioning course allowed students to compare their own decision-making with an AI-generated alternative, reflecting the demands of safety-critical industries where professional judgement cannot be outsourced. New Model Institute for Technology and Engineering’s (NMITE) James Atuonwu contributes two case studies, “Authentic Tutorial Questions” and “Triadic Socratic Learning”, which position AI as, in his words, ‘a contestable interlocutor rather than an authoritative source’ within hands-on thermofluids experiments.

ESCP Business School London built a bespoke dialogue-based chatbot, Amélie, to help students revise French coursework, after an earlier experiment saw students use AI simply to generate corrected text rather than understand their mistakes.

Other case studies address the operational pressures facing smaller providers. David Game Higher Education in London, replaces a patchwork of spreadsheets with a self-built ‘admissions hub’, using generative AI for workflow design while deliberately avoiding new software subscriptions, arguing that enterprise systems are often disproportionately expensive for institutions of this size.

Building bridges to business

Employability and industry engagement also feature prominently. The University Academy 92’s TechFest programme pairs computer science and cyber security students with industry mentors ahead of a public showcase. At Ravensbourne University London, colleagues ran hackathon-style pilots matching student engineers with startup founders, leading to paid work for some participants. In Wales, Bridgend College partnered with St Fagans National Museum of History so electrical engineering students could design lighting for historic buildings, addressing what the project describes as a heritage skills gap in the construction trades.

Inclusion runs through several contributions too. For example, Elizabeth School of London examine how assessment design can inadvertently disadvantage multilingual adult learners, while separately introducing anonymous, scenario-based ‘Knowledge Sprints’ to surface misunderstandings among working adults in real time.

Nick Skeet, Director of Membership & Global Development at Advance HE said: “We’re delighted to share the case studies from this year’s Innovative Practice Grant awardees. The scheme gives smaller institutions a platform to share their innovations, and many of the insights are applicable across higher education institutions of all shapes and sizes.

title: heise-Angebot: Software-Architektur zwischen KI, Innovation und digitaler Souveränität
summary: Die OOP 2027 ist „Beyond the Hype“: Über 120 Sessions zeigen, welche Trends, Technologien und Ideen Softwareprofis wirklich weiterbringen.
full_text:
Inhaltsverzeichnis

Beyond the Hype: Was bleibt, wenn der Hype vorbei ist?

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

KI, neue Technologien und ständig neue Trends verändern die Software-Entwicklung in rasantem Tempo. Doch welche Entwicklungen sind tatsächlich relevant für die Praxis – und welche erweisen sich als kurzfristiger Hype? Mit ihrem Motto „Beyond the Hype“ stellt die OOP 2027 genau diese Frage in den Mittelpunkt.

Seit 35 Jahren bringt die OOP Software-Architekten, Entwickler:innen, IT-Verantwortliche und weitere IT-Professionals zusammen, um aktuelle Entwicklungen einzuordnen, Erfahrungen auszutauschen und gemeinsam über die Zukunft der Software-Entwicklung nachzudenken. Auch 2027 geht es dabei nicht darum, jedem neuen Trend möglichst schnell zu folgen. Vielmehr steht die Frage im Mittelpunkt, wie sich Innovation, Machbarkeit, Sicherheit und nachhaltiger Mehrwert miteinander verbinden lassen.

Über 120 Vorträge, Keynotes und Workshops

Das frisch veröffentlichte Programm umfasst mehr als 120 Vorträge, Keynotes und Workshops an vier Tagen. Bis zu sieben parallele Tracks eröffnen dabei unterschiedliche Perspektiven auf die Herausforderungen, vor denen Software-Teams und Unternehmen heute stehen.

Ein Schwerpunkt liegt auf der Frage, wie KI-native Software-Architekturen und agentenbasierte Systeme das Systemdesign verändern. Der Track „AI Beyond the Hype“ richtet den Blick dabei bewusst auf konkrete Transformationen: Was geht über Experimente hinaus und wird tatsächlich zu einem produktiven Bestandteil der Software-Entwicklung?

Gleichzeitig reicht das Programm weit über KI hinaus. Es geht um Architektur, Design und Programmierung, um Testen und Qualität, Führung in einer sich verändernden IT-Arbeitswelt sowie um die Frage, welche Grundlagen auch angesichts neuer Technologien Bestand haben.

Digitale Souveränität und Resilienz

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Ein weiterer Akzent liegt auf der zunehmenden politischen und technologischen Unsicherheit. Der Track „Digital Sovereignty in Practice“ beschäftigt sich damit, wie Systeme und Organisationen resilienter werden können und welche Konsequenzen Abhängigkeiten von Technologien, Plattformen und Anbietern für die IT haben.

Damit verbindet die OOP technische Fragestellungen mit den Rahmenbedingungen, unter denen Software heute entsteht und betrieben wird. Neben theoretischen Grundlagen stehen dabei Fallstudien, Workshops und praxisorientierte Sessions im Mittelpunkt.

Für wen lohnt sich der Blick ins Programm?

Das Themenspektrum richtet sich längst nicht nur an klassische Software-Architekten. Interessant ist die OOP 2027 unter anderem für Software-Entwickler, Product Owner und Agile Coaches, IT-Entscheider und CTOs, Projektleiter und Team Leads sowie Qualitätsverantwortliche und Tester.

Gerade die große thematische Breite ermöglicht es auch Teams mit unterschiedlichen Rollen und Schwerpunkten, auf derselben Konferenz passende Inhalte zu finden – und anschließend über gemeinsame Fragestellungen ins Gespräch zu kommen.

Rund 150 Experten aus dem In- und Ausland gestalten das Programm. Ergänzt wird das Vortragsangebot durch eine Ausstellung mit Softwareherstellern, Serviceanbietern und IT-Dienstleistern.

Wer wissen möchte, ob die OOP 2027 zu den eigenen fachlichen Schwerpunkten passt, kann sich deshalb am besten selbst ein Bild machen: Das vollständige Konferenzprogramm mit mehr als 120 Sessions ist jetzt online.

OOP Konferenz by heise

Die OOP Konferenz by heise gehört seit mehr als 35 Jahren zu den etablierten Fachkonferenzen für Software-Architektur und Software-Entwicklung im deutschsprachigen Raum. Sie bringt Software-Architekten, Entwickler:innen, IT-Entscheider und weitere IT-Professionals zusammen, die sich mit der Gestaltung moderner Softwaresysteme und den Herausforderungen der digitalen Zukunft beschäftigen.

Im Mittelpunkt steht ein breites, von der Community kuratiertes Fachprogramm mit mehr als 120 Vorträgen, Keynotes und Workshops. Rund 150 Experten aus dem In- und Ausland geben Einblicke in aktuelle Entwicklungen, teilen Erfahrungen aus der Praxis und diskutieren unterschiedliche Perspektiven auf Technologie, Architektur und Organisation.

Die OOP verbindet dabei technologische Tiefe mit konkreter Praxiserfahrung. Neben aktuellen Themen wie Künstlicher Intelligenz, KI-nativen Architekturen und agentenbasierten Systemen geht es um grundlegende Fragen von Softwarearchitektur, Design und Programmierung ebenso wie um Testing und Qualität, Agilität, Führung und digitale Souveränität.

Unter dem Motto „Beyond the Hype“ richtet die OOP 2027 den Blick bewusst hinter die aktuellen Schlagzeilen: Welche Innovationen schaffen tatsächlich Mehrwert? Wie lassen sich neue Technologien mit Stabilität, Sicherheit und Machbarkeit verbinden? Und welche Prinzipien bleiben auch dann relevant, wenn der nächste Hype längst da ist?

Zielgruppe & Teilnahme

Die OOP richtet sich an Software-Architekten, Software-Entwickler:innen, Product Owner und Agile Coaches, IT-Entscheider und CTOs, Projektleiter und Team Leads sowie Qualitätsverantwortliche und Tester.

Bis zu sieben parallele Tracks ermöglichen es, individuelle fachliche Schwerpunkte zu setzen und gleichzeitig über den eigenen Themenbereich hinauszublicken. Ergänzt wird das Konferenzprogramm durch eine Ausstellung mit Software-Herstellern, Serviceanbietern und IT-Dienstleistern sowie zahlreiche Möglichkeiten zum persönlichen Austausch innerhalb der IT-Community.

Termin: 02. - 05. Februar 2027

Ort: SCC München

Motto: „Beyond the Hype“

Programm: mehr als 120 Vorträge, Keynotes und Workshops in bis zu sieben parallelen Tracks

title: El avance de la extrema derecha en redes
summary:
¿Falla la educación digital? | Carles Feixa

La entrada El avance de la extrema derecha en redes se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
En esta emisión especial de InfoCLACSO, conversamos con el destacado antropólogo y especialista en estudios sobre juventudes, Carles Feixa, para reflexionar críticamente sobre el papel de las nuevas generaciones en América Latina y el Caribe frente a los dilemas tecnológicos, políticos y culturales del presente.

A lo largo de la entrevista, Feixa analiza los siguientes ejes centrales:

Más allá del marketing generacional: Frente a los discursos que estigmatizan o simplifican a la juventud de 20 años bajo etiquetas comerciales y de mercado, se propone una mirada sociológica profunda que reconozca la diversidad de realidades, las desigualdades estructurales y la agencia política de los jóvenes en la región.

full_text:
Come si gestiscono i risparmi? E come si riconosce una truffa finanziaria prima di perdere denaro? Sono domande poste dagli studenti a dare origine al nuovo percorso del liceo scientifico dell’IISS «Don Giovanni Colletto» di Corleone. La curvatura economico-finanziaria è stata inaugurata dopo un anno di lavoro per inserirla nel programma di studi. La scuola aveva già raccolto le adesioni delle famiglie degli iscritti alle prime classi per l’anno scolastico 2026-2027.

L’obiettivo è dare continuità all’educazione finanziaria, portando tra i banchi conoscenze utili per le decisioni quotidiane: valutare una proposta, comprendere i rischi legati al denaro, proteggere i propri risparmi. A seguire il progetto sarà un comitato tecnico-scientifico formato da insegnanti dell’istituto, rappresentanti del mondo bancario e docenti del Dipartimento di Scienze economiche, aziendali e statistiche dell’Università di Palermo.

All’inaugurazione ha partecipato Davide Passero, amministratore delegato di Alleanza Assicurazioni. Il rapporto con la scuola era cominciato nel maggio 2025, quando Passero aveva incontrato gli studenti per discutere di alfabetizzazione finanziaria e inclusione sociale. Da quel confronto, e dalle richieste dei ragazzi, la dirigente Elisa Inglima e il collegio dei docenti hanno sviluppato un percorso inserito nel curricolo.

La collaborazione con Alleanza è stata formalizzata in occasione dell’avvio della sperimentazione. La compagnia coprirà i costi del personale docente specializzato e istituirà una borsa di studio per gli studenti più meritevoli al termine del primo biennio. «Un elemento di particolare qualificazione per il nostro liceo e per l’intero territorio», afferma Inglima.

Il divario con il resto del Paese cresce sulla conoscenza del sistema pensionistico, dove l’Isola si ferma a 42 punti contro 48. title: L’ASN finisce nel dimenticatoio
summary: L’ASN finisce nel dimenticatoio dopo 15 lunghi anni. full_text:
L’ASN finisce nel dimenticatoio dopo 15 lunghi anni. Vi sono stati, infatti, Settori Concorsuali nel quali abilitarsi era quasi impossibile, in particolare se si finiva nel tritacarne delle vendette trasversali fra baroni, nel mentre in altri Settori si abilitavano praticamente tutti. Ha “riorganizzato”, in peggio, l’intero comparto della ricerca universitaria, fatto ora solo di prodotti della ricerca, convegni e seminari, riviste di classe A, indici bibliometrici, pubblicazioni a pagamento, crescita esponenziale delle citazioni, ma anche, più in generale, di articoli e saggi. Tutto questo accadrà di nuovo, purtroppo, perché l’ASN è stata soppiantata da una procedura “a semaforo”, nella quale gli studiosi presenteranno una dichiarazione sostitutiva di certificazione del possesso di requisiti che verranno individuati con apposito Decreto ministeriale. Il capitolo sulla composizione delle commissioni giudicatrici fa apparire l’estensore della norma come un soggetto che non ha mai frequentato un ufficio universitario. Perché non si è introdotto il divieto di far parte delle Commissioni nei primi tre anni di servizio, in modo da evitare che i neofiti possano immediatamente selezionare i loro colleghi, evidentemente sdebitandosi? Perché è stata introdotta l’incandidabilità solo a seguito di condanne passate in giudicato? Infine, un tempo non era consentito “cucire addosso” al candidato il bando per consentirgli di vincere, prima ancora di cominciare, la selezione. Oggi tale circostanza entra dalla porta principale e temo che il rimedio sia stato peggiore del male.

L’ASN finisce nel dimenticatoio dopo 15 lunghi anni. Significativa è la circostanza che a decretarne la morte sia la proposta di una Ministra (Bernini) appartenente al medesimo partito politico di chi la volle (Gelmini).

Sulla bontà, validità, efficacia e, soprattutto, equità dell’Abilitazione sono stati spesi fiumi d’inchiostro e questo mio intervento si limiterà a formulare alcune elementari considerazioni sul suo (distorto) funzionamento, sia dal punto di vista diacronico, sia dal punto di vista sincronico. Vi sono stati, infatti, Settori Concorsuali nel quali abilitarsi era quasi impossibile, in particolare se si finiva nel tritacarne delle vendette trasversali fra baroni, nel mentre in altri Settori si abilitavano praticamente tutti. Ve ne sono stati alcuni nei quali l’agognato risultato giungeva dopo un lungo contenzioso giurisdizionale (anche questo con alterne vicende) e altri, invece, i cui risultati apparivano già decisi prim’ancora delle riunioni d’insediamento.

L’ASN doveva essere, almeno nelle intenzioni del legislatore e di chi fra noi l’ha criticata, ma accettata, una mera “constatazione” del possesso di requisiti e pubblicazioni tali da consentire di partecipare alla selezione vera, rappresentata dal concorso locale e non una forca caudina talvolta insuperabile per alcuni e un’autostrada in discesa per altri.

Ma essa ha avuto, come pure è stato molto opportunamente notato taluni commentatori anche su questo sito, conseguenze importanti che hanno “riorganizzato”, in peggio, l’intero comparto della ricerca universitaria, fatto ora solo di prodotti della ricerca, convegni e seminari, riviste di classe A, indici bibliometrici, pubblicazioni a pagamento, crescita esponenziale delle citazioni, ma anche, più in generale, di articoli e saggi. Mi è personalmente capitato di scorrere la produzione scientifica di un collega di area giuridica che in biennio ha dichiarato di aver pubblicato 30 contributi, di cui 20 in classe A, circostanza che francamente nessuna persona di buon senso può considerare come ragionevole e corretta.

Tutto questo accadrà di nuovo, purtroppo, perché l’ASN è stata soppiantata da una procedura “a semaforo”, nella quale gli studiosi presenteranno una dichiarazione sostitutiva di certificazione del possesso di requisiti che verranno individuati con apposito Decreto ministeriale. Tutto si fonderà, conseguentemente, sotto il profilo “quantitativo” e nessuna Commissione nazionale potrà giudicare la bontà e la qualità della produzione scientifica, passando ai raggi x ogni singola pubblicazione. Da questo punto di vista se si voleva eliminare la discrezionalità (buona o cattiva) delle Commissioni Nazionali di Abilitazione, l’obiettivo mi parrebbe esser stato pienamente raggiunto.

Tutti i candidati, quindi, in possesso della vecchia ASN o dei nuovi requisiti sono legittimati, di conseguenza, a partecipare alle selezioni locali, procedura su cui la nuova legge mi sembrerebbe essere intervenuta in maniera talvolta piuttosto timida, talaltra introducendo veri e propri buchi neri in grado di minare la trasparenza delle procedure medesime.

Il capitolo sulla composizione delle commissioni giudicatrici locali viene affrontato e modificato (si passa da 3 a 5 commissari, sorteggiati su base nazionale da liste di docenti dichiaratisi disponibili e in possesso di precisi requisiti), ma si è evitato di incidere in maniera più pregnante sulle loro dinamiche, quasi da far apparire l’estensore della norma come un soggetto che non ha mai frequentato un ufficio universitario. Perché non si è reintrodotto (come un tempo) il divieto di far parte delle Commissioni nei primi tre anni di servizio, in modo da evitare che i neofiti possano immediatamente selezionare i loro colleghi, evidentemente sdebitandosi? Perché è stata introdotta l’incandidabilità solo a seguito di condanne passate in giudicato (come è noto abrogato l’abuso d’ufficio, salvo rari casi, i concorsi universitari non temono i procedimenti penali)? Perché non sono stati introdotti meccanismi sanzionatori nei confronti di quelle Commissioni di concorso i cui esiti sono stati rovesciati dalla giurisprudenza amministrativa?

Resta, infine, l’infelice possibile interpretazione di quella parte della nuova legge che consentirebbe di introdurre una profilazione puntuale e precisa nel bando (un tempo si diceva della possibilità di “cucire addosso” al candidato il bando per consentirgli di vincere, prima ancora di cominciare, la selezione). Qui il legislatore ha commesso un grave e temo irrimediabile errore che è destinato a rendere praticamente inutile tutta la procedura: un tempo non era consentito e talvolta il giudice sanzionava gli Atenei, oggi tale circostanza entra dalla porta principale ed è destinata a far discutere. Su questo punto temo che il rimedio sia stato peggiore del male.
